chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
title: Right-hand technique and the fanning motion on fast tempos
summary: They discuss plucking with two fingers, the fan motion bassists used on fast tunes, and the thumb brace.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Now, in those days -- now, I've seen films of bass players when they played in the '30s. And now, do you, when you're playing pizzicato, do you use your first and second finger on your right hand?
Well now, I've seen films where these guys look like, it looks like they're doing almost like a circular kind of a motion with one hand, with the right hand, like up tempo things.
I saw a thing right with Oscar Pettiford in a film that --
-- with Coleman Hawkins, now, and it looked like he was playing a bass, looked like he was fanning the bass.
Now, whereas today, though, when the
guys play fast, almost all of the motion, you can see almost all of the motion in the first two fingers rather than the fanning kind of a motion.
Now, were most of the guys using, for lack of a better term, the fanning kind of approach, like that, when you were coming along?

Yeah, that's the way I used to do it, and I still do it, kind of a fan. When I'm playing a very fast number, it's kind of a, you know, fan effect. And, of course, lots of bass players use the side of the fingerboard for a brace with their thumb, and extend while they pluck that string.
Oh, pluck with the first two fingers, yes.

First two fingers, yeah, but that thumb is a brace, while when you just use your two fingers, first two fingers, in the fan effect, you just got to know where to hit those, the right strings at the right time, you know.
